Abstract (198 words)

::: {custom-style="Abstract"}
Prognostic models are essential for providing individual survival predictions. We aimed to investigate the uncertainty of survival predictions from the Cox proportional hazards model using the concept of effective sample size ($N_{*}$). Effective sample size translates prediction variance into a number of 'patients like you' that a prediction is effectively based on. Properties of $N_{*}$ were investigated in a real-world example of colon cancer patients. Simulation studies clarified the behavior of variance components stemming from baseline hazard and coefficient estimation. Remarkably, the efficiency of the Cox model allows $N_{*}$ to exceed the total development sample size ($N$) during early follow-up. While this surplus reflects the model's efficiency, it can be perceived as misleading in risk communication with patients. When a large proportion of the total events in the development data had occurred (e.g. \>50%), $N_{*}$ became a more intuitive measure of uncertainty. Additionally, $N_{*}$ may be a valuable diagnostic tool for the investigation of individual uncertainty during model development to guard against modeling covariate profiles with high uncertainty. In conclusion, the complex properties of Cox model variance mean that while $N_{*}$ is a valid indicator of uncertainty, its use in patient communication is only appropriate during later follow-up.
:::

## 1 Introduction

Prognostic models with survival outcomes are widespread in clinical domains such as oncology and cardiology. Examples are the Melanoma Institute Australia models which provide survival predictions for patients at different stages of melanoma,[@pires2022; @varey2024] the PREDICT model for breast cancer treatment decision support,[@predict] and the QRISK3 algorithm predicting the 10-year risk of cardiovascular disease.[@qrisk] Effective implementation and presentation of personalized prognoses supports shared decision-making by addressing the informational needs of both patients and clinicians.[@vromans2021; @4Dpicture]

Uncertainty is an important element of predictions from prognostic models.[@riley2025] Uncertainty in predictions has been used as an argument for and against shared decision-making.[@pieterse2026] Many risk calculators make no mention of prediction uncertainty,[@pires2022; @qrisk] while some show 95% confidence intervals around predicted survival probabilities[@varey2024] or treatment benefit.[@predict] Guidelines such as the TRIPOD+AI[@collins2024] statement advise developers to consider sample size requirements to ensure a minimum level of prediction certainty. More recently, focus has shifted to the stability of models and the uncertainty in individual predictions.[@riley2025; @altman1989; @shen2016; @riley2023; @riley2023b; @barrenada2025]

Effective sample size has been suggested as a promising summary measure of individual uncertainty in generalized linear models and machine learning models.[@thomassen2024; @thomassen2025] Effective sample size for a patient's prediction translates the prediction variance to the number of patients with the same covariate values that the prediction was effectively based on. In survival analysis, the concept provides a readily interpretable measure for Kaplan-Meier curves, where it is based on the local information available within the risk set.[@kaplanmeier1958; @hackmann2025] Extending this concept to survival predictions based on multiple prognostic factors using the Cox proportional hazards model presents a new challenge.

We hypothesize that effective sample size can be used to express individual uncertainty for multivariable survival predictions. For this measure to be useful in clinical practice, we investigate two requirements:

1.  Intuitive behavior: Effective sample size reflects the size of a sample with complete follow-up and does not exceed the total sample size.
2.  Reflection of exceptionality: Effective sample size reflects the exceptionality of a patient profile within the development data.

This paper describes the calculation of effective sample size for the Cox model (Section 2), applies it to a colon cancer dataset (Section 3), and uses simulations to explore its behavior in depth (Section 4). In the discussion (Section 5), the effective sample size is interpreted with respect to the statistical properties of the Cox model, and potential applications in model development and risk communication are considered.

## 2 Effective sample size for the Cox model

### 2.1 Effective sample size

We consider the Cox proportional hazards model, a semi-parametric survival model in which the hazard function is defined as $h\left( t|x \right) = h_{0}(t)\exp\left( \beta^{\top}x \right)$, with cumulative hazard $H\left( t|x \right) = \int_{0}^{t}h\left( u|x \right) = H_{0}(t)\exp\left( \beta^{\top}x \right)$.[@cox1972]

Suppose we observe $N$ independent individuals with data $(T_{i},Y_{i},x_{i}),$ with $i = 1,\ldots,N,$ where $T_{i}$ is the observed time and $Y_{i} \in \{ 0,1\}$ is the event indicator (1 = event, 0 = censored). Let $t_{1} < \ldots < t_{l}$ denote the distinct ordered event times, and let $d_{j}$ be the number of events occurring at time $t_{j}$. For each event time $t_{j}$, define the risk set $R_{j} = R\left( t_{j} \right) = \{ i:T_{i} \geq t_{j}\}$.

Suppose that we have fitted a Cox proportional hazards model on $(T_{i},Y_{i},x_{i}),$ with $i = 1,\ldots,N,$ yielding estimated cumulative baseline hazard ${\widehat{H}}_{0}(t)$ and estimated coefficient vector $\widehat{\beta} = \left( {\widehat{\beta}}_{1},\ldots,{\widehat{\beta}}_{p} \right)$. The personalized survival prediction for a new patient at a predetermined time $t$ using this Cox model is ${\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t) = \widehat{S}\left( t|x_{\text{new}} \right) = exp\left( - {\widehat{H}}_{0}(t)\exp\left( {\widehat{\beta}}^{\top}x_{\text{new}} \right) \right)$, based on their covariate values $x_{\text{new}} = \left( x_{1},\ldots,x_{p} \right)$ .

To define the effective sample size for this patient at time $t$, we take as a reference the situation where we have a number $N_{*}$ patients with identical distributed outcomes who all have the same covariate values $x_{\text{new}}$ as the new patient and are followed from time 0 to $t$ without loss to follow-up. Suppose we would have obtained in this virtual sample the same survival estimate ${\widehat{S}}_{N_{*}}(t) =$ ${\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t)$ for the binary outcome survived until time t, yes/no. Then the binomial sampling variance could be estimated by $V_{\text{Bin}}\left( {\widehat{S}}_{N_{*}}(t) \right) = \frac{{\widehat{S}}_{N_{*}}(t)\left( 1 - {\widehat{S}}_{N_{*}}(t) \right)}{N_{*}}$. To calculate effective sample size, we equate the variance of the Cox model prediction ${\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t)$ with the binomial sampling variance of the sample mean outcome ${\widehat{S}}_{N_{*}}(t)$:

$$V_{\text{Cox}}\left( {\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t) \right) = V_{\text{Bin}}\left( {\widehat{S}}_{N_{*}}(t) \right)\ \quad(1)$$

We can calculate the number $N_{*}$ as the number of patients required to obtain the same uncertainty in our estimate of ${\widehat{S}}_{N_{*}}(t)$, as in the model estimate of ${\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t)$. This number $N_{*}$ is the effective sample size. We can estimate $N_{*}$ using:

$$N_{*}: = \frac{{\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t)\left( 1 - {\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t) \right)}{V_{\text{Cox}}\left( {\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t) \right)}\quad(2)$$

where $V_{\text{Cox}}\left( {\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t) \right)$ is the estimated variance of the Cox model survival estimate for the new patient at time $t$. The variance of the Cox model survival estimate can be estimated through several methods. A standard estimator is based on the delta method,[@tsiatis1981; @andersen1993] which is implemented in frequently used software for survival analysis (details in Supplement 2).[@package-survival; @mstate2011] Using the delta method variance estimator, effective sample size for a Cox model prediction of a patient with covariate values $x_{\text{new}}$ at time $t$ is:

$$N_{*}\left( t,x_{\text{new}} \right) = \frac{{\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t)\left( 1 - {\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t) \right)}{\exp\left( 2{\widehat{\beta}}^{\top}x_{\text{new}} \right){\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}^{2}(t)\left\lbrack \sum_{i:t_{i} \leq t}^{}\frac{d_{i}}{\left( \sum_{j \in R_{i}}^{}\exp\left( {\widehat{\beta}}^{\top}x_{j} \right) \right)^{2}} + w^{\top}I\left( \widehat{\beta} \right)^{- 1}w \right\rbrack},\quad(3)$$

where $w = \left( w_{1},\ldots,w_{p} \right)$ is a vector of partial derivatives, with $w_{q}$ the partial derivative of the survival function in the direction of $\beta_{q}$ for $q \in \{ 1,\ldots,p\}$ with:

$$w_{q} = \sum_{i:t_{i} \leq t}^{}\frac{d_i}{\sum_{j \in R_{i}}^{}\exp\left( {\widehat{\beta}}^{\top}x_{j} \right)}\left( {\overline{x}}_{q} - x_{\text{new},q} \right),\quad(4)$$

with ${\overline{x}}_{q}$ the risk-weighted average of $x_{q}$ in the population (Supplement 2).

Other methods exist for estimating the variance, such as the Von Mises expansion,[@vandervaart1998; @riskRegression] or the infinitesimal jackknife.[@survival-vignette] Any of these methods can be applied for estimating effective sample size using Equation (2).

### 2.3 Interpretation

The effective sample size of a Cox model survival prediction is determined by the variance of the estimated prediction, which comprises two components: the uncertainty in the estimated survival probability given the coefficients, and the uncertainty in the estimated coefficients. One difference between the Cox model and nonparametric setting is that the count of patients at risk is replaced by the sum of risk scores.[@therneau2000] In a survival setting without covariates, the Nelson-Aalen estimator for the cumulative hazard is:[@nelson1972; @aalen1978]

$$\widehat{H}(t) = \sum_{j:t_{j} \leq t}^{}\frac{d_{j}}{n_{j}},\ \ \ (5)$$

where $d_{j}$ is the number of events at time $t_{j}$ and $n_{j}$ is the number of patients at risk. Every patient at risk at time $t_{j}$ contributes exactly 1 to the denominator: $n_{j} = \sum_{i \in R_{j}}^{}1$.

The cumulative baseline hazard of the Cox model is commonly estimated using the Breslow estimator:[@breslow1974]

$${\widehat{H}}_{0}(t) = \sum_{j:t_{j} \leq t}^{}\frac{d_{j}}{\sum_{i \in R_{j}}^{}\exp\left( {\widehat{\beta}}^{\top}x_{i} \right)}.\ \ \ \ \ (6)$$

While at risk, each patient contributes a weight equal to their risk score, $\exp{\left( {\widehat{\beta}}^{\top}x_{i} \right),\ \ }$ to the denominator at all $t$, because of the proportional hazards assumption.While the Nelson-Aalen estimator of the cumulative hazard is an aggregate over time, its hazard increments $(\Delta\widehat{H}\left( t_{j} \right) = \ \frac{d_{j}}{n_{j}})$ are purely local, relying only on the count of individuals at risk at a specific time $t_{j}$. In contrast, the estimated hazard increments from the Breslow estimator utilize the estimated coefficients $\widehat{\beta}$ which are derived from the entire follow-up period.

Because $\widehat{\beta}$ is estimated using all events across the entire follow-up period, the model effectively uses information of events that occur after $t_{j}$ to estimate the baseline hazard estimate at $t_{j}$. For many patients, specifically those with risk scores close to or below the risk-weighted mean of the population, this global estimation of $\widehat{\beta}$ results in a lower prediction variance than the local counting process used in the Nelson-Aalen estimator (Supplement 3).

In addition, there is variance in the estimated coefficients, $V\left( \widehat{\beta} \right) = \ I\left( \widehat{\beta} \right)^{- 1}$. This variance is linked to the survival estimate through the gradient of the survival function with respect to the coefficients, captured in $w$ (Equation (4)). This gradient depends on the distance between a patient's covariates $x$ and the risk-weighted mean of the covariates. For patients with exceptional covariate profiles far from the population mean, the gradient is larger, which increases variance and reduces $N_{*}$. This risk-weighted mean reflects the composition of the risk set $R(t)$ at time $t$. The risk set evolves over time as patients experience the event or are censored and the risk-weighted mean changes with it. The exceptionality of a patient profile is therefore time-dependent.

### 2.4 Software

All analyses were conducted in R,[@R] version 4.5.1, using the packages survival[@package-survival] and mstate.[@mstate2011] Simulations were run using the simsurv package.[@package-simsurv] Code used for this article, including functions that can calculate the effective sample size for a `survfit.coxph` object in R can be found on GitHub: <https://github.com/survival-lumc/EffectiveSampleSize_Cox>.

## 3 Application to colon cancer data

### 3.1 Data description

We performed analyses in the colon data set as available within the survival package[@package-survival] in R. This data set contains colorectal cancer patients who underwent a curative resection and were enrolled in a randomized controlled trial. Treatment arms were adjuvant levamisole ('Lev'); levamisole+5-fluorouracil ('Lev+5FU'); or untreated as a control arm ('Obs').[@laurie1989; @moertel1995] Survival was the primary outcome for 929 patients, with recurrence-free survival as secondary outcome.

Four baseline prognostic factors were considered in this study: treatment as randomized ('rx', 3 categories); tumor adherence to adjacent organs ('adhere', 2 categories); age ('age', continuous); and number of positive lymph nodes ('nodes', continuous, Supplement 4). The data example is used for illustration purposes only.

### 3.2 Illustration with one predictor

We compared Cox models with a single categorical predictor to Kaplan-Meier curves for the two categorical variables 'rx' and 'adhere'. At early time points, the Cox model yielded substantially higher effective sample sizes than the stratified Kaplan-Meier curves. Remarkably, the effective sample size for the Cox model predictions exceeded the total development sample size for early survival estimates in the Lev+5FU treatment arm and the "no adherence" group. This unintuitive surplus ($N_{*} > N$) decreased as events accumulated over the follow-up period (@fig-1). The higher effective sample size for the Cox model predictions corresponded with narrower confidence intervals compared to Kaplan-Meier estimates, particularly early in follow-up (Supplement 6).

Next, we illustrate the properties of $N_{*}$using a single continuous covariate. For patients of median age, the effective sample size remained close to the total population size until the onset of censoring (@fig-2). For those at the 75th or 99th percentiles, the estimated effective sample size initially decreased and remained stable until six years of follow-up, in line with censoring occurring mainly after six years. While survival predictions were similar for all three example patients due to the minor prognostic impact of age (HR 1.02 \[95% CI 0.93 -- 1.13\] per SD increase), the uncertainty was notably larger for those with rare age profiles.

We observed a similar phenomenon for the number of nodes. Patients with the median value (2 nodes) had $N_{*} > N$. For a patient with 17 nodes, the effective sample size increased slightly over time with the survival probability approaching zero (@fig-2).

### 3.3 Effective sample size in multivariable Cox models

Cox model predictions are typically based on multiple predictors and presented as survival probabilities at specific time points. We fit four sequential models and make 5-year survival predictions for all patients in the development data to investigate the impact of increasing complexity: (A) treatment; (B) treatment and tumor adherence; (C) treatment, adherence, and number of positive nodes; and (D) treatment, adherence, nodes, and age (@fig-3). With each additional predictor, the median effective sample size ($N_{*}$) in the development population decreased: 337 for model A, 329 for model B, 325 for model C, and 253 for model D.

The addition of adherence to a model based only on treatment changed the predicted probabilities and substantially reduced $N_{*}$ for the smaller category of patients with tumor adherence, though its impact on median $N_{*}$ was small. Similarly, the number of nodes decreased $N_{*}$ for many patients while increasing the spread in predictions, yet the median $N_{*}$ remained relatively stable. In contrast, the inclusion of age resulted in only a minor increase in the spread of predictions while introducing substantial heterogeneity in $N_{*}$ and a large decrease in median $N_{*}$. Indeed, age was a weak predictor (delta Cox-Snell $R^{2}\ 0.15\%$) of the survival outcome, whereas the number of nodes was a much stronger predictor (delta Cox-Snell $R^{2}\ 7.7\%$).

## 4 Investigation of effective sample size in simulations

### 4.1 Simulation setting

We conducted two simulation studies to evaluate the behavior of effective sample size ($N_{*}$).

The first simulation study investigated $N_{*}$ early on in follow-up in a large dataset ($N = 10,000$) without censoring. We simulated a constant baseline hazard ($h_{0}(t) = 1$) and considered a single predictor: either a binary indicator $X_{1}$ (with exactly half the population assigned $X_{1} = 1$) or a continuous variable $X_{2} \sim N(0,1)$. In both scenarios, the hazard ratio (HR) was set to $2$.

The second simulation study evaluated how $N_{*}$ behaved in late follow-up. We simulated a dataset ($N = 1,000$) where survival times followed a Weibull distribution (shape $\gamma = 0.5$). The same predictor $X_{1}$ from the first simulation study was used again. Weibull scale was varied across simulations to achieve specific event incidences at the end of follow-up ($t_{end} = 10$). We performed 100 replications for each scenario.

Detailed technical specifications and the code required for full reproducibility are provided in the Supplementary Materials and on Github: <https://github.com/survival-lumc/EffectiveSampleSize_Cox>.

### 4.2 Behavior early in follow-up

In the first simulation study, Cox model-based survival estimates yielded higher effective sample sizes than the actual number of patients in each group. For the binary predictor, $N_{*}$ started at $15,000$ for the low-risk group ($X_{1} = 0$) and $7,500$ for the high-risk group ($X_{1} = 1$), despite both groups containing exactly $5,000$ patients (@fig-4).

Decomposing the variance revealed that this high $N_{*}$ was driven almost entirely by the variance attributable to the baseline hazard estimation early in follow-up (Figure 4C). Because the Cox model utilizes global information from all events to estimate the baseline hazard, it provided a more precise estimate than the local Kaplan-Meier approach. The surplus $N_{*} > N$ is caused by the efficiency of the Cox model in comparison to the reference binomial experiment.

For the continuous predictor $X_{2}$, $N_{*}$ exhibited significant heterogeneity; while patients at the mean ($X_{2} = 0$) initially had an $N_{*}$ above the total population size, those with above average risk scores ($X_{2} = 1$) had a rapid decrease in $N_{*}$ over time with their survival probability decreasing (@fig-5).

Notably, equally unique patients, such as those with $X_{2} = 1$ and $X_{2} = - 1$, did not share the same effective sample size. This asymmetry occurred because their different survival probabilities and different gradients with respect to the coefficient over time resulted in distinct $N_{*}$ trajectories. Specifically, as follow-up progressed, the relative impact of coefficient uncertainty evolved differently for high-risk versus low-risk profiles. High-risk individuals are more likely to experience the event and leave the risk set. This further separates their effective sample sizes despite their equal distance from the population mean.

### 4.3 Behavior late in follow-up

The second simulation study demonstrated that $N_{*}$ decreases toward the actual sample size of the category based on the relative proportion of events observed before time $t$, $\left( \frac{\sum_{j:t_{j} \leq t}^{}d_{j}}{\sum_{j:t_{j} \leq t_{end}}^{}d_{j}} \right)$. The Cox model $N_{*}$ approached the Kaplan-Meier $N_{*}$ estimate when the number of events approached the total number of events available in the development data (@fig-6 and 7). When the survival probability at the end of follow-up was below 50%, the effective sample size at the end of follow-up became larger than the Kaplan-Meier $N_{*}$. With very low survival probabilities (\<20%), effective sample size can become very high, e.g. for the group with HR=2.

## 5 Discussion

This study shows that effective sample size behaves in a complicated way for the Cox proportional hazards model. We relate our findings to the criteria set in the introduction.

1.  Intuitive behavior: Effective sample size for Cox model predictions only partly reflects the size of a sample with complete follow-up. The effective sample size may start out higher than the total sample size. Without censoring, the effective sample size of Cox model predictions based on a single binary variable decrease towards the Kaplan-Meier effective sample size based on the relative number of events (@fig-6). With censoring, effective sample size also decreases in line with the pattern seen in Kaplan-Meier effective sample size (@fig-1). Additionally, effective sample size increases when survival probabilities become low (\<20%; @fig-4, @fig-7).

2.  Reflection of exceptionality: Effective sample size reflects the commonality of a patient profile within the development data. This criterium is met as shown in @fig-3. Patients with common profiles, such as the median age, have an effective sample size similar to the total sample size in the absence of censoring, while patients with exceptional covariate values have a low effective sample size. This behavior was not symmetric however, as patients with similar exceptionality (covariate value of 1 SD from the mean value) had quite different effective sample sizes due to different survival probabilities (@fig-5).

### 5.2 Efficiency of the Cox model

The finding that effective sample size ($N_{*}$) for the Cox model may exceed the total development sample size $N$ requires further reflection. This observation may reflect the model's informational efficiency relative to the binomial distribution used as a reference for the variance of $S(t)$.

A driving force of this efficiency is the proportional hazards assumption, which allows for the global estimation of coefficients ($\beta$) over the entire follow-up period.[@cox1972; @efron1977] Calculating $N_{*}$ involves equating the Cox model prediction variance with binomial sampling variance. This comparison implicitly suggests one could achieve the same precision as the model by conducting a binomial experiment on $N_{*}$ clones of the patient. Because the binomial experiment relies on the outcome at a single point in time, it is less efficient than the Cox model, which extracts more information from the data by using the timing of all events. Comparisons of the Cox model to logistic regression demonstrate this increased efficiency (Supplement 11).[@green1983; @annesi1989] Cox model predictions yield narrower confidence intervals than logistic regression predictions, but maintain nominal 95% coverage if the model is well-specified (Supplement 11, 13). However, this increased efficiency carries a potential cost related to model misspecification. The surplus of $N_{*}$ over development $N$ is predicated on the validity of the proportional hazards assumption.

### 5.3 Effective sample size in model development

The addition of covariates to a Cox model had different impacts on the spread of predictions and their corresponding effective sample sizes (@fig-3). This illustrates that a balance must be struck between bias and variance when making individual predictions. For example, the addition of age to the model resulted in only minor changes to predicted probabilities yet substantially decreased $N_{*}$ for older and younger patients. During development, such trade-offs must be considered.

Recent sample size guidelines focus on reliable estimation of the average risk and limiting overfitting. For instance, a minimum of 100 patients may be recommended to estimate an overall event rate with a 20% relative uncertainty of ±0.1.[@steyerbergbook; @harrellblog] Furthermore, managing model complexity has historically relied on rules of thumb, such as 10 to 15 events per variable (EPV) for proportional hazards regression.[@peduzzi1995; @harrellbook] These general rules have faced criticism[@vansmeden2016; @riley2019] and primarily ensure that the model is well-specified on average.

As a diagnostic tool, $N_{*}$ provides an individualized complement to these global metrics. As exemplified in @fig-3, specific individuals can exhibit very low effective sample sizes even while the median effective sample size is adequate. This allows developers to identify covariate profiles where predictions are deemed too uncertain for clinical decision-making. To mitigate these risks, modelers might consider winsorizing continuous covariate values[@royston2000; @aguinis2013] or implementing penalized prediction methods to stabilize estimates in the tails of the predictor distributions.[@houwelingen1990; @verweij1994]

Guidelines for acceptable effective sample size are inherently context dependent. However, we suggest that in addition to meeting global sample size requirements, modelers should aim for a median $N_{*}$ of at least 100 to ensure adequate certainty for most of the population.[@harrellblog] Additionally, $N_{*}$ of at least 10 might be a minimum for any individual covariate profile.[@thomassen2024]

### 5.4 Communication of effective sample size

Effective sample size intends to be an interpretable metric for communicating uncertainty in clinical predictions. For linear models, generalized linear models, machine learning, and Kaplan-Meier estimates, the measure may serve as an intuitive supplement to, or replacement for, standard 95% confidence intervals.[@thomassen2024; @thomassen2025; @hackmann2025] Extending this metric to the Cox model appears to be more nuanced.

Communication of model results is especially important for shared decision-making for preference-sensitive clinical decisions.[@stiggelbout2015] Implementing this collaborative process requires decision support tools such as prognostic models.[@4Dpicture] These models carry inherent uncertainty that may need to be communicated for a fair informed deliberation.[@4Dpicture; @pieterse2026] Communicating such uncertainty may undermine trust to some extent, even if the impact is small.[@fischhoff2012; @vanderbles2020] Transparency is particularly relevant when risks are framed using frequency statements, such as: "If we had 100 patients like you, we would expect X to survive".[@kattan2002] In this context, $N_{*}$ can be used to qualify the denominator, specifying that the estimate is not based on an arbitrary 100 individuals, but effectively on $N_{*}$ patients. This approach combines risk communication with an estimate of uncertainty. Future research is needed to determine a preferable format for clinical communication.

For direct communication with patients, effective sample sizes larger than the development sample size $N$ remain problematic. Notably, this behavior is most prominent in early follow-up. As shown in @fig-6, $N_{*}$ behaves better later in the follow-up period, particularly once \>50% of the total events in the development data have been observed. Additionally, $N_{*}$ can increase as the survival probability approaches 0. It generally remains close to the expected Kaplan-Meier $N_{*}$ when $S(t) > 0.2$ (@fig-7). If effective sample size is considered for the communication of Cox model predictions, we recommend a thorough investigation of $N_{*}$ behavior for the specific model.

## 6 Conclusion

Effective sample size ($N_{*}$) for the Cox model is a complex measure for quantifying the uncertainty of individual survival predictions. By incorporating both event status and timing, the Cox model leverages more information from the patient timeline than the discrete binomial experiment underlying the $N_{*}$ metric.[@efron1977; @green1983] Unlike the Kaplan-Meier setting, where $N_{*}$ is constrained by the sample size of a specific stratum,[@hackmann2025] the proportional hazards assumption enables a more efficient estimation of survival probability. This informational efficiency allows $N_{*}$ to mathematically exceed the actual development sample size ($N$).

While this surplus follows directly from the statistical properties of the estimator, it may be difficult to interpret in risk communication during early follow-up when few events have been observed. The measure provides meaningful clinical insights merely at later time points, specifically after more than a substantial proportion of the events in the development data have occurred and when survival probability is not approaching 0. Future research should evaluate the impact of $N_{*}$ on patient perception of uncertainty in risk communication and its utility in guiding model development decisions.

The reduction in $N_{*}$ is governed by the proportion of total events (C) observed rather than absolute time (A) or absolute event count (B). Estimates converge toward a minimum as the available longitudinal information is consumed.](images/fig6.png){#fig-6}

![Final effective sample size ($N_{*}$) as a function of predicted event incidence ($1 - S(t)$). For lower event incidences, $N_{*}$ at the end of follow-up equilibrates with the Kaplan-Meier estimate. However, for high predicted incidences (>50%), the informational efficiency of the proportional hazards model causes $N_{*}$ to remain above the Kaplan-Meier baseline, with sharp increases observed at incidences exceeding 80%.](images/fig7.png){#fig-7}
